## Part 1 · 00:00

[00:00] In a small garden just outside ancient Athens, a philosopher gathered a community dedicated to a simple but ambitious goal to understand the nature of the world and to live peacefully within it. We must exercise ourselves in the things which bring happiness since if that be present, we have everything and if that be absent, all our actions are directed toward attaining it. They explored nature to understand its workings and reflected on ethics to guide their lives. They nurtured friendship and cherished thoughtful conversation.

[00:41] And above all, they sought freedom from unnecessary pain, especially the pain caused by fear and confusion. Much of it rooted in the religious beliefs that dominated Greek society. This way of life might seem modest, but in a society where divine forces were believed to control everything from weather to illness to morality and even the afterlife, it was something extraordinary.

[01:13] In this video, we'll explore how Epicurius developed a philosophy that challenged fear-based religion, sought to explain the world through nature, not myths, and offered an ethics grounded in human well-being, an approach that has helped shape modern ideas of happiness, reason, and personal freedom. Let's dive in. Epicurius was born in 341 B.CE on the island of Seamos, a Greek colony in the eastern Aian Sea. He lived in a world deeply shaped by the intellectual traditions of Plato and Aristotle.

[01:41] Philosophy and their legacy often revolved around abstract systems, ideal forms, divine purpose, cosmic hierarchies, and the search for truths beyond what the senses could perceive. Greek society was deeply rooted in religious ritual and structured by clear social hierarchies. Life was shaped by tradition, civic duty, and a strong sense of divine presence. For many, uncertainty and fear of the gods, of misfortune, of death were part of daily experience. Epicurius took a different path. He wasn't interested in ideal forms or celestial mechanics.

[02:12] He didn't write about the soul's place in a divine cosmos or the moral order of the universe. His focus was more grounded and more personal. He wanted to understand how human beings could live well, how they could think clearly, free themselves from fear, and find lasting peace in a world that offered no guarantees. It is useless to attend lectures on natural science if you fear the thunderbolts and the gods. Empty is the argument of the philosopher which does not relieve any human suffering. If you wish to be happy, do not seek to increase your goods, but to lessen your desires.

[02:52] It was informal, welcoming, and open to people typically excluded from philosophical circles, women, former slaves, and ordinary citizens. This alone speaks to something important about his character. He was less interested in status or power, and more interested in helping people live better lives. For Epicurius, philosophy wasn't a career or a system. It was a medicine for the soul, a way to replace confusion with clarity, fear with understanding, and restlessness with contentment. His philosophy came down to a simple equation. Don't fear the gods. Don't fear death. Understand nature.

[03:34] Limit your desires. That's the path to happiness. Now, let's be clear. Epicurius wasn't an atheist in the modern Dawkins style sense. He didn't go around trying to abolish religion or declare that gods didn't exist. In fact, he said there are gods for the knowledge of them is self-evident. But here's the twist. The gods don't care. To Epicurius, the gods exist in some remote blissful state. perfect beings who don't interfere, don't judge, and certainly don't punish. The blessed and immortal nature knows no trouble itself and brings no trouble upon any other being.

[04:14] He wasn't trying to erase religion or campaign against it. He was trying to rescue people from what religion had become, a system built on fear, guilt, and ritualized anxiety. And that's where he drew the line. Epicurius wasn't anti- good. He was anti-fear, anti-substition, anti- authority masquerading as divine truth. He redefined piety not as sacrifice or obedience, but as emulating the gods peace, not fearing their wrath. In other words, he didn't reject spirituality. He rejected the weaponization of belief. The gods weren't watching. They weren't judging. They weren't punishing.

[04:54] This was radical in a time when people sacrificed animals to appease Zeus and saw eclipses as omens of divine anger. Epcurious offered a different message. Fear comes from misunderstanding and understanding nature is the first step towards peace of mind. He believed fear of the gods and especially of death was paralyzing humanity. So he offered a liberating view. When we die, there's no afterlife, no punishment, no reward, just nothing. Accustom yourself to believe that death is nothing to us. For all good and evil consists in sensation, and death is the privation of sensation.

[05:38] Therefore, a correct understanding that death is nothing to us makes the mortality of life enjoyable, not by adding infinite time, but by removing the longing for immortality. For there is nothing terrible in life. For the man who has truly understood that there is nothing terrible in not living. So foolish, therefore, is the man who says that he fears death not because it causes him pain when it is present, but because he suffers in anticipation, for that which while present causes no distress, causes unnecessary pain when merely anticipated.

[06:19] Rather than seeing the end of life as something to fear, Epicuri saw it as a source of liberation. If death is simply the absence of sensation, if there is no afterlife, no judgment, no eternal punishment, then we are free to stop worrying about what comes next. What mattered for Epicurius was this life, the one we're living now. And in this life, Epicurius offered a somewhat radical claim for the time. The world wasn't governed by intention. It also wasn't out to get us. It simply was. Epicurius offered a coherent vision of the universe grounded in observation, not myth.

[06:55] He believed that peace of mind depended on more than just letting go of fear. It required knowing how the world actually works. It is impossible to dispel fear about the most important matters. If one does not understand the nature of the universe, but without this understanding, there is no peace. To explain the world, he turned to atomism, a theory first proposed by Democrus. But Ebicurius wasn't just borrowing old ideas. He reworked them into something more practical.

[07:36] Reality, he said, consists of atoms and void, tiny indivisible particles moving through empty space, forming and dissolving all things by chance and necessity. Even the soul was made of atoms. There was no divine order shaping events from above, no cosmic justice unfolding behind the scenes, just the movement of matter in infinite combinations. We must suppose that the elements out of which worlds and all things in them are composed are limited in number and that these elements are indivisible and unchangeable. These elements are of solid substance and cannot be dissolved in any way.

[08:08] Nothing exists except atoms and empty space. Everything else is opinion. We must consider that the whole nature of the soul is a body composed of fine particles dispersed throughout the body. The gods are not the cause of all things. For if they were, all things would be perfect. To many this might sound cold or bleak, but to Epicurus it was liberating. The idea that the universe is indifferent, not hostile, not judgmental, meant that we could stop looking for meaning in what were thought to be supernatural forces and start finding it in what we can observe, experience, and understand.

[08:50] Natural causes, not angry gods, were behind the lightning, the plague, the harvest. And by understanding these causes, even imperfectly, we free ourselves from fear. Not because we control the world, but because we no longer misinterpret it. This shift from divine explanation to natural cause wasn't just a philosophical position. It was a form of therapy. Because if nature runs its own terms and we are part of it, then the good life isn't about appeasing higher powers. It's about learning to live wisely within the natural order.

[09:28] Epicurious ideas might have vanished entirely if not for the Roman poet Lucriccius who centuries later distilled his philosophy into a sweeping poetic work called on the nature of things. Lucriccius expanded the core principles of Epicurian philosophy atomism the denial of divine intervention to morality of the soul and the pursuit of tranquility through reason. Thanks to the biographer Dioynes Liosherus, we also have three of Epicurious letters along with the principal doctrines and Vatican sayings, brief pointed reflections on ethics, nature, fear, and freedom.

## Part 2 · 10:06

[10:06] These fragments preserve Epicurious voice with remarkable clarity. But it was Lucriccia's poem that turned his philosophy into poetry and preserved Epicurianism long enough to be rediscovered. In the 15th century, a manuscript of on the nature of things was found in a monastery by Italian humanist Poio Bratulini just as Europe was beginning to break from religious dogma and look to classical sources for guidance. Its reappearance came at a critical moment.

[10:42] The poem's naturalism, its vision of a universe governed by material processes, not divine will, helped fuel the early modern shift toward science, secular ethics, and intellectual freedom. His ideas found new life in early modern philosophy and political thought. Thomas Jefferson, the United States third president and one of the founding fathers, openly called himself an Epicurion and was inspired by the philosophy's embrace on happiness, reason, and freedom from fear.

[11:08] While his political vision drew from many sources, Epicuri shaped his belief that the good life should be grounded in personal well-being and individual liberty. In this sense, the Eburian framework has to a large extent helped shape democratic values and political ideals.

[11:38] When Jefferson wrote in the Declaration of Independence of the United States of America that the purpose of government was to secure life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness, he echoed the Epicuran conviction that pleasure, not in the shallow sense, but in the form of peace and fulfillment, is the proper goal of life, and thus must be the core principles upon which the new nation was to be built. Epicurus didn't invent modern science or democracy, but his ideas helped make both imaginable.

[11:55] Even though Epicurius placed pleasure at the center of his philosophy, he wasn't a hedonist in the wild party all night sense. He preached moderation. For Ibicurius, pleasure meant freedom from pain, both physical and mental. What really made life good? friendship, reflection, a simple life with minimal desires. If you wish to be rich, do not add to your money, but subtract from your desires. We don't often hear his name, but the influence of Epicurius is quietly woven into the fabric of modern life. He challenged the fears that held people hostage in his time.

[12:32] Fear of the gods, of death, of things beyond our control. And he offered something in their place. peace of mind. His philosophy wasn't loud or political. It was personal, modest, practical, a way to live without fear, without illusion, and without needing more than what is truly enough. And it all began in a small garden on the edge of Athens. A quiet space where anyone, regardless of status or background, could come to think, question, and live differently. In our age of noise, urgency, and uncertainty, his message still resonates. Seek understanding. Live simply, nurture friendships.

[13:14] Let go of what you can't control. And take joy calmly in the life that is yours.
